Finally, using the power rule for logarithms (a square root is a power of one half), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}& -\log_{5}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)-\log_{5}\left(z^{4}\right)+\log_{5}\left(y^{2}\right) \\ &= -\frac{1}{2}\log_{5}\left(x\right)-4\log_{5}\left(z\right)+2\log_{5}\left(y\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{5}\left(\frac{y^{2}}{\sqrt{x}z^{4}}\right) \\ &= -\frac{1}{2}\log_{5}\left(x\right)-4\log_{5}\left(z\right)+2\log_{5}\left(y\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Assume $x,y,z>0$.

Express $3\log_{2}\left(y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)-4\log_{2}\left(x\right)$ as a single logarithm.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Using the power rule for logarithms, we can rewrite the terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}& 3\log_{2}\left(y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)-4\log_{2}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right)+\log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we combine the factors with the same sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right)+\log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{4}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{4}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{4}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& 3\log_{2}\left(y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)-4\log_{2}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{4}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.

The laws of logarithms are:

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)+\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(ab\right)$ — the product rule

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)-\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ — the quotient rule

- $\log_{n}\left(c^{m}\right)=m\log_{n}\left(c\right)$ — the power rule

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(\frac{y^{3}}{\sqrt{x}z^{5}}\right) \\ &= \log\left(y^{3}\right)-\log\left(\sqrt{x}z^{5}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(y^{3}\right)-\log\left(\sqrt{x}z^{5}\right) \\ &= -\log\left(z^{5}\right)-\log\left(\sqrt{x}\right)+\log\left(y^{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the power rule for logarithms (a square root is a power of one half), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}& -\log\left(z^{5}\right)-\log\left(\sqrt{x}\right)+\log\left(y^{3}\right) \\ &= -5\log\left(z\right)-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(x\right)+3\log\left(y\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(\frac{y^{3}}{\sqrt{x}z^{5}}\right) \\ &= -5\log\left(z\right)-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(x\right)+3\log\left(y\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Assume $x>0$.

Express $-3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right)$ as a single logarithm.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Using the power rule for logarithms, rewrite the powered numerical term and evaluate the power:

$$
\begin{aligned}& -3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right) \\ &= -\log_{3}\left(2^{3}\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right) \\ &= -\log_{3}\left(8\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, combine the factors with the same sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}& -\log_{3}\left(8\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(8x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quotient rule for logarithms and simplifying the numerical factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(8x\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(\frac{4}{8x}\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& -3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(4\right)-\log_{3}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2x}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x>0$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Assume $x,y,z>0$.

Express $-2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right)$ as a single logarithm.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Using the power rule for logarithms, we can rewrite the terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}& -2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right) \\ &= -\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right)+\log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)+\log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we combine the factors with the same sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}& -\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right)+\log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)+\log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& -2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.
